summary: Gives recommendations for software that automatically responds to email, such as vacation replies and mail filters. It aims to discourage behavior that causes mail loops or floods, for example replying to mailing lists or to messages that were themselves automatic.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives guidance for software that replies to email automatically. It explains when to stay silent, how to address and label a reply, and how to reduce loops and unwanted disclosure.

questions: how should vacation auto replies work
out of office email best practices
how to avoid email auto reply loops
where should an out of office reply be sent
subtitle: Guidance for automatic mail responders to avoid loops, unwanted replies, and unsafe disclosures.

tldr.problem: Automatic email responders can send useless replies, reply to inappropriate addresses, disclose information, or trigger mail loops.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC recommends when responders should remain silent, where they should send replies, how to format them, and how to mark automated messages with Auto-Submitted.
tldr.outcome: Mail software can recognize automated responses and reduce unwanted traffic, though the recommendations cannot prevent every attack. RFC 3834 is updated by RFC 5436.

today: RFC 3834 is a Proposed Standard, published in August 2004, and is updated by RFC 5436. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Types of Automatic Responders
sections.content:
Automatic responders include vacation notices, email information services, challenges, and mail filters. The RFC distinguishes service responders, which provide an email service, from personal responders for one recipient and group responders for many recipients.

Different responders have different purposes. A personal responder should assume a person will read its reply and should send a brief plain-text response. Delivery Status Notifications and Message Disposition Notifications follow their own specifications when the message qualifies for them.
sections.plainLanguage: Automatic responders serve different roles, so the same reply rules do not fit every one. Personal and group responders should keep replies brief and readable by people.

sections.title: When a Responder Should Stay Silent
sections.content:
A responder MUST NOT reply blindly to every message. Automatic responses SHOULD NOT be sent to messages marked with an Auto-Submitted value other than no. Personal and group absence notices SHOULD NOT be repeated to the same sender within several days; seven days is the recommended default.

A personal or group absence notice should be sent only when the recipient's address appears in a recipient field. A responder MUST NOT send a reply to a null return address. It may also skip mailing-list traffic or reply only to correspondents it trusts.
sections.plainLanguage: A responder should check the message before replying. It should avoid replying to other automated mail, repeating an absence notice too often, or sending to a return address that cannot receive mail.

sections.title: Headers and Content of the Reply
sections.content:
The From field should identify the person or service on whose behalf the response was sent and provide a way to contact its maintainer. A personal responder MUST let the recipient choose the name and address used in From. A response should have one To recipient, and its Date field should show when the response was generated.

The Subject should briefly identify an automatic response; Auto: may be used as a prefix, but software MUST NOT treat that prefix as proof of automation. Replies SHOULD include Auto-Submitted: auto-replied. Personal and group replies SHOULD be brief, plain text, and should not include significant original content or attachments.
sections.plainLanguage: The reply should identify who it represents and clearly say that a process generated it. It should go to one recipient and avoid copying substantial content from the original message.

sections.title: Choosing the Reply Destination
sections.content:
A response generated after delivery SHOULD go to the message's Return-Path. A response generated before delivery SHOULD go to the reverse-path from SMTP MAIL FROM. If Return-Path is missing after delivery, a personal or group responder SHOULD NOT guess another address.

Personal and group responders SHOULD NOT use From, Reply-To, or Sender as the destination. Those fields can name a mailing list, several people, or an address that is not suitable for automatic replies. A service responder may use another address only when its service specification defines that behavior precisely.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the message's return address for an automatic reply. Do not guess from the visible sender fields, because they may direct the reply to a group or an unsuitable address.

sections.title: The Auto-Submitted Field
sections.content:
Auto-Submitted tells receiving software that a message came from an automatic process rather than a person. A message may contain at most one such field. The values include no, auto-generated, and auto-replied, with optional extension values and parameters.

Use auto-generated for automatic messages that are not direct replies, such as periodic jobs. Use auto-replied for a message sent in direct response to another message. The field SHOULD NOT be added to manually submitted messages, and implementations MUST accept syntactically valid optional parameters.
sections.plainLanguage: This field identifies mail created by software. Its value distinguishes an automatic response from an automatic message that was not sent as a reply.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
Automatic responders can relay harmful content, flood mailboxes, create loops, reveal whether an address is valid, disclose personal information, or be overwhelmed by requests. The recommendations to limit replies, avoid relaying original content, and mark automated responses reduce these risks but do not eliminate them.

Email return addresses can be forged. Automatically generated information SHOULD NOT disclose personal details that the sender could not already readily obtain. A responder that does not restrict access or require authentication remains open to attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: Attackers can use automatic replies to spread content, flood inboxes, or learn private details. Clear labels and limits reduce harm, but forged addresses mean some risk remains.
